title: How digital payments work, and getting ready safely

say: How digital payments work, and getting ready safely.
This is the video for module 1 of Digital Payments and POS Basics.
A digital payment is any payment where no cash changes hands. A number in one account goes down, and a number in another goes up. The money is real, just stored as a record.

say: For example, Chioma in Enugu owes her tailor, Ada, 7,500 naira. She opens her banking app, taps Transfer, types Ada's 10-digit account number and chooses Ada's bank.

Receiver's bank credits her account
Both of you get alerts

say: The app shows the name ADA N. OKAFOR. This is called a name enquiry, and it is your most important safety check. If the name is not who you expect, stop. Close enough is not enough.

say: Ada does not trust a screenshot. She opens her own app and sees the 7,500 naira in her balance. That is the only real proof.
Chioma keeps her receipt and the session ID, a long number she will need if anything goes wrong.

say: Anyone can edit a picture of a receipt, and SMS alerts can be faked. When you receive money, check your own balance before you release goods or give change.

say: Digital payments give you control, reach, less cash on the road, and records. Your transaction history is a free notebook that keeps itself.

card.title: What a month of transfers shows

say: Ngozi's app shows 38,000, then 41,500, then 29,000, then 45,500 naira received by transfer.

card.title: What a month of transfers shows

say: That is 154,000 naira for the month. Her cash sales? She cannot tell, because she wrote nothing down.
A statement like this can prove your income to a lender.

say: Cash is not free. For example, Amina in Kaduna must pay a rice wholesaler 80,000 naira.
In cash, a POS agent charges to withdraw it, say 1,600 naira in this practice example, plus 1,000 for transport. 2,600 in all, and the risk of carrying cash.

panel.heading: Paying a wholesaler 80,000 naira
left: Cost 2,600, and risk on the bus

say: By transfer, her screen shows a practice charge of 50 naira, plus the same transport. That is 1,050, with a record. Always read the real fee on your screen before you confirm.

panel.heading: Paying a wholesaler 80,000 naira
left: Cost 2,600, and risk on the bus

say: A bank app needs a smartphone and data. A USSD code works on any phone with no data, so it is your backup when data runs out.

panel.heading: Different doors, one account
items: Bank app transfer: needs data
USSD code: any phone, no data
Debit card at POS or ATM: no data
Wallet app, QR code, payment link

say: Your card works at a POS or ATM without data. Wallets, QR codes and links need internet.
They are all doors into the same account. Anyone who gets through one door with your PIN can reach the whole balance.

say: Open the account in your own name, with your own active phone number. If an old SIM is linked, change it at the bank, because OTPs go to whoever has that number now.

Turn on alerts and check your limits
Save the official customer care number

say: Install the app yourself, from the Play Store or App Store, and check the publisher is the real company.

say: Choose a 4-digit PIN that is not your birth year, phone number, or a pattern like 1234 or 0000. Do not write it on your card.

say: Turn on alerts for every transaction, check your account level and limits in the app, and save your bank's customer care number from the back of your card.

say: Your account number is safe to share. Your PIN, password and OTP are never shared with anyone, including someone who says they work for your bank, or a husband or close friend.

panel.rule: Never share your PIN, password or OTP, even with bank staff.

say: To remember. Check the name before you confirm. Your own balance is the only true proof. Read the fee on the screen before you pay. Large or distant payments are usually safer by transfer. And keep your PIN private, even within the family.
